title: Checklist-completers retain at nearly double — make it mandatory?

scenario.role: You're the product analyst at Plotline
scenario.situation: Plotline shows new users an optional onboarding checklist. Sam, the PM, pulled the numbers and is convinced it's the key to retention: users who complete the checklist retain at 60% over 30 days versus 34% for those who don't — nearly double. He wants to make the checklist mandatory, gating the app until it's done, and expects that to pull the non-completers up to completer-level retention. He needs your analysis first.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Finishing the checklist nearly doubles 30-day retention. If we force everyone to complete it, we'll bring the rest up to ~60% too."
scenario.question: Is completing the checklist what drives the retention, or the other way round? Estimate the checklist's real effect and tell Sam whether making it mandatory will lift retention.

columns.name: signup_source
columns.description: How the user arrived: organic, paid, or referral

columns.name: setup_actions_first_hour
columns.description: Number of setup actions the user took in their first hour — BEFORE the checklist — a signal of how motivated they arrived

columns.name: completed_checklist
columns.description: 1 if the user finished the onboarding checklist, else 0

columns.name: retained_30d
columns.description: 1 if the user was still active 30 days later, else 0 — the outcome

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Sam's number: 30-day retention for checklist-completers vs non-completers. How big is the gap?
Who completes the checklist? Compare setup_actions_first_hour — the pre-checklist motivation signal — for completers vs non-completers.
Completing the checklist is voluntary. If motivated users both complete it AND retain anyway, which direction does the causation run?
Estimate the checklist's effect holding intent constant — stratify on setup_actions_first_hour (deciles) or model retained_30d ~ setup_actions + completed_checklist. What's left?
Sam wants to gate the app on completion. Given who the non-completers are, will forcing them through the checklist give them the completer's retention?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the headline gap so you know the exact claim.
Before crediting the checklist, describe who finishes it: compare the pre-checklist intent signal across completers and non-completers.
This is a self-selection setup — users opt in. If the opt-in signal also predicts retention, it confounds the raw comparison.
Adjust for intent (stratify on setup_actions or model it) and see how much of the gap survives.

Reason about the intervention: mandatory completion changes who completes, not who's motivated — forecast against the adjusted effect, and note that a randomised forced-vs-optional test would settle it.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Checklist-completers retain at 60.5% versus 33.5% for non-completers — a +27 point gap, nearly 1.8x. Read directly, the checklist looks like the strongest retention lever Plotline has, and forcing it looks like a free way to lift the non-completers to ~60%.
teachingNote.theTrap: Completing the checklist is voluntary, so completers self-selected. The users who bother to finish it arrived more motivated: they took 7.4 setup actions in their first hour on average, versus 4.9 for non-completers. That early intent is what drives retention — the same motivation that makes someone finish the checklist also makes them stick around. The checklist is a marker of intent, not mainly a cause of retention. Comparing completers to non-completers compares motivated users to unmotivated ones and blames the difference on the checklist.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Hold intent constant — stratify on first-hour setup actions and compare completers vs not within each stratum (or model retained_30d ~ setup_actions + completed_checklist) — and the checklist's effect shrinks to about +4.6 points. Real and worth a nudge, but a sixth of the headline. Making the checklist mandatory forces low-intent users to click through it; it does not give them the motivation the voluntary completers already had, so it will not pull them from 34% to 60%. Expect a few points at most. If Sam wants a trustworthy number, randomise: force the checklist for half of new users and compare.
howToGetThere: Compute the naive gap: retention for completed_checklist=1 (60.5%) minus =0 (33.5%) → +27.0 pts (~1.8x).
Profile who completes: mean(setup_actions_first_hour) by completion → ~7.4 vs ~4.9. Completers arrived more motivated.
Recognise self-selection: setup_actions proxies intent, which drives BOTH completion and retention, inflating the raw gap.
Adjust — stratify on setup_actions deciles and take the size-weighted within-stratum difference, or fit retained_30d ~ setup_actions + completed_checklist. The effect lands near +4.6 pts.
Reason about the policy: forcing completion moves the click, not the motivation — the honest effect, not the gap, is what a mandate would buy.
teachingNote.lesson: When users opt into a behaviour, comparing the opt-ins to everyone else measures who they already were, not what the behaviour did. Motivated users complete onboarding AND retain; the checklist rides along as a marker. Before turning a voluntary behaviour into a mandate, ask whether the people doing it were different to begin with — and adjust for that difference. Here a nearly-2x story becomes a few-points one. A mandate changes who completes without changing who's motivated, so it can't reproduce the self-selected gap. The only clean read is to randomise the requirement and compare.
